section.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Haploidentical Transplant and the Beijing Protocol
section.intro: These questions explain what a haploidentical (half-matched) stem cell transplant is, how the Beijing Protocol works, and why it can offer a treatment path for blood cancer patients who do not have a fully matched donor. Final decisions always rest with the treating transplant team.

groups.title: Understanding Haploidentical Transplant and the Beijing Protocol

items.q: What is a haploidentical stem cell transplant?
items.a: A haploidentical stem cell transplant is a transplant using a donor who is a 50% (half) genetic match, usually a parent, child, or sibling. It replaces diseased bone marrow with healthy donor stem cells for blood cancers such as leukaemia, lymphoma, and myelodysplastic syndrome. Because only a half-match is needed, almost every patient has a potential family donor. Suitability depends on diagnosis, disease status, age, and transplant team assessment.

items.q: What is the Beijing Protocol for haploidentical transplant?
items.a: The Beijing Protocol is a widely used haploidentical transplant method developed at Peking University that uses granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) primed bone marrow and blood stem cells, without removing T-cells from the graft. It relies on intensive immune-suppressing medicines to control complications rather than costly cell-processing equipment. Many centres in Asia and worldwide use variations of this approach. Its appropriateness for any patient is decided after specialist review.

items.q: How does a haploidentical transplant differ from a matched donor transplant?
items.a: A haploidentical transplant uses a half-matched family donor, while a matched transplant uses a fully compatible sibling or unrelated donor. The main difference is a higher risk of immune complications, which modern protocols like the Beijing Protocol or post-transplant cyclophosphamide are designed to manage. Outcomes in experienced centres can be comparable for selected patients, but results vary by cancer type, disease stage, and overall health.

items.q: Why does haploidentical transplant matter for patients without a matched donor?
items.a: Haploidentical transplant matters because it gives a transplant option to patients who cannot find a fully matched sibling or unrelated donor. Only about one in four patients has a matched sibling, and unrelated donor searches can fail, especially for people from ethnic minority backgrounds. Since a half-matched relative is almost always available, treatment can start faster. Whether transplant is right depends on diagnosis, disease control, and specialist evaluation.

items.q: Who is eligible for a haploidentical transplant?
items.a: Eligibility for a haploidentical transplant depends on the type and stage of blood cancer, disease response to earlier treatment, age, organ function, and overall fitness. It may be considered for leukaemia, lymphoma, myelodysplastic syndrome, and certain other conditions when a transplant is indicated but no matched donor exists. A half-matched relative must be available and healthy enough to donate. Final eligibility is confirmed only after full transplant team assessment.

items.q: Who can be a half-matched donor?
items.a: A half-matched (haploidentical) donor is usually a biological parent, child, or sibling who shares 50% of tissue-typing markers. Parents and children are almost always half-matches, and siblings have a high chance of being suitable. The donor must pass health screening, infection testing, and tissue-typing before donation. When several relatives qualify, the team selects the best donor based on age, sex, blood type, and immune-matching factors.

items.q: How does the haploidentical transplant process work?
items.a: The haploidentical transplant process begins with conditioning chemotherapy, sometimes with radiation, to clear diseased marrow and suppress the immune system. Donor stem cells are then infused and travel to the bone marrow to produce healthy new blood cells, a stage called engraftment. Immune-suppressing medicines help prevent complications during recovery. The full process typically involves several weeks in hospital followed by close monitoring, with timelines varying by patient.

items.q: What are the risks and side effects of haploidentical transplant?
items.a: The main risks of haploidentical transplant include graft-versus-host disease (GvHD), where donor cells attack the patient's tissues, along with infections, low blood counts, and organ strain from conditioning treatment. The half-match raises GvHD risk, which is why protocols use careful immune suppression. Side effects range from mild to serious and are managed by the transplant team. Risks should be discussed in detail with a qualified oncology and transplant team.

Success rates for haploidentical transplants have improved significantly and, in experienced centres, can approach those of matched donor transplants for selected patients. Outcomes depend heavily on cancer type, disease status at transplant, patient age, and complications such as GvHD or infection. No transplant guarantees a cure, and results differ between individuals. A realistic outlook should be discussed with the treating transplant specialists based on the patient's specific situation.

items.q: How much does a haploidentical transplant cost?
items.a: The cost of a haploidentical transplant varies widely by country, hospital, and individual case. In many international centres, estimated costs often range from around USD 40,000 to USD 120,000 or more, but this is only a guide. Final cost depends on diagnosis, conditioning protocol, length of stay, complications, medicines, and follow-up care. Patients should request a detailed written estimate from the treating hospital before planning treatment.

items.q: Which countries offer haploidentical transplant using the Beijing Protocol?
items.a: Haploidentical transplants, including Beijing Protocol approaches, are performed in China, India, and several other countries with established transplant programmes. China has extensive experience given the protocol's origin, while many centres in Asia, Europe, and elsewhere use haploidentical methods. Availability and expertise vary between hospitals. Choice of country and centre should be based on programme experience, patient condition, and advice from the treating medical team.

items.q: Is haploidentical transplant available in India?
items.a: Yes, haploidentical transplant is available in India at several major transplant centres with experienced teams. India performs a growing number of half-matched transplants for leukaemia, lymphoma, and related blood disorders, often at lower cost than many Western countries. Availability, waiting times, and protocols differ between hospitals. Whether it is suitable for a particular patient depends on diagnosis, disease status, donor availability, and transplant team assessment.

items.q: How can international patients access a haploidentical transplant?
items.a: International patients can access haploidentical transplant by sharing their medical reports with a transplant centre for review, arranging donor tissue-typing, and obtaining a treatment plan and cost estimate. Access depends on hospital acceptance, medical suitability, donor availability, visa approval, and fitness to travel. Coordination of second opinions, appointments, and travel can help, but admission and treatment are never guaranteed and remain subject to the treating team's evaluation.

items.q: What is the difference between the Beijing Protocol and post-transplant cyclophosphamide?
items.a: The Beijing Protocol and post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) are two leading approaches to haploidentical transplant that manage immune complications differently. The Beijing Protocol uses G-CSF-primed grafts with intensive immune suppression, while PTCy gives high-dose chemotherapy shortly after transplant to reduce harmful donor T-cell activity. Both are widely used with good results in selected patients. The choice depends on centre experience, patient factors, and transplant team judgement.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for haploidentical transplant?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials for haploidentical transplant are ongoing to refine protocols, reduce GvHD, and improve outcomes for different blood cancers. Some trials combine transplant with newer immune therapies or modified conditioning. Eligibility is decided only after medical record review and investigator assessment, and trials often have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Participation does not guarantee benefit, and enrolment is never assured. A patient's transplant team can advise on suitable options.

items.q: Can haploidentical transplant be combined with CAR-T or other therapies?
items.a: In some cases, haploidentical transplant may be considered alongside or after other therapies such as CAR-T cell therapy, targeted drugs, or immunotherapy, depending on the cancer type and disease control. These combinations are used in selected patients and often within specialist centres or clinical trials. Whether such an approach is appropriate depends on diagnosis, prior treatment, biomarker profile, and careful review by the treating oncology and transplant team.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to plan a haploidentical transplant?
items.a: Planning a haploidentical transplant usually requires a confirmed diagnosis with pathology and bone marrow reports, recent blood counts, imaging, treatment history, and details of disease response. Tissue-typing (HLA) results for the patient and potential family donors are essential. Infection screening and organ function tests are also needed. The exact requirements vary by centre, and the transplant team will confirm which reports are needed after an initial review.

items.q: How long does recovery after a haploidentical transplant take?
items.a: Recovery after a haploidentical transplant varies, but patients often stay in hospital for several weeks until blood counts recover and early complications are controlled. Immune recovery continues for many months, during which infection risk remains higher and close monitoring is essential. Many patients need to stay near the transplant centre for a period after discharge. Recovery timelines differ by individual and should be discussed with the treating team.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with haploidentical transplant?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant transplant specialists or centres, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, donor evaluation, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology and transplant team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, disease status, donor availability, previous treatment, and overall health. Hospital admission, donor suitability, and treatment outcomes cannot be guaranteed.
